Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review useful imaging modalities available for the evaluation of rotator cuff disease, including
radiography, ultrasonography, MRI, and CT arthrography.
Discuss the indications, diagnostic utility, and potential shortcomings of each imaging modality
in the diagnosis of rotator cuff disease.
Perform an appropriate radiographic work up of patients in whom rotator cuff disease is
suspected.

The rotator cuff is pivotal to proper function of the glenohumeral joint, introducing
dynamic stability via mechanical force coupling that maintains concentric reduction of
the humeral head on the glenoid while allowing for a wide range of motion. Rotator cuff
disease encompasses a wide spectrum of pathology that is defined by abnormal
architecture and/or function of the supraspinatus, subscapularis, infraspinatus, and/or
teres minor. Rotator cuff pathology may affect motion within the glenohumeral joint,
resulting in pain, weakness, and loss of function. The incidence of rotator cuff disease
increases with age and may have extrinsic and intrinsic factors (Resource 1) .
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patient history and physical examination are crucial in the evaluation of shoulder pain or
dysfunction.
A thorough patient history and physical examination of the shoulder should be carried out
before advanced imaging studies of the shoulder are obtained because they may aid in
determination of the diagnosis and additional management.
Imaging Studies
Although the patient history and physical examination are pivotal in the evaluation of any
shoulder problem, imaging studies of the rotator cuff are highly useful in the diagnosis and
management of rotator cuff disease.
Imaging modalities that can be used to evaluate for rotator cuff disease include radiography,
ultrasonography, CT, CT arthrography, and MRI.
Radiography
A standard shoulder series should include a true AP view in the scapular plane, an AP view, an
axillary view, and a scapular-Y view (Figure 1).

Figure 1
AP (A) and axillary (B) radiographs of a left shoulder. The axillary view demonstrates a
posterior glenohumeral dislocation that was radiographically occult on the AP view. (Courtesy
of Joseph T. Labrum IV, MD, Nashville, TN, and Ian R. Byram, MD, Franklin, TN.)
Calcification observed within the rotator cuff insertion is known as rotator cuff calcific
tendinopathy.
Caused by calcium carbonate apatite deposition within the rotator cuff tendon (Figure 2)

Figure 2
AP radiograph of a left shoulder demonstrates rotator cuff calcific tendinitis. Radiographic
findings are caused by calcium carbonate apatite deposition within the rotator cuff tendon.
(Courtesy of Joseph T. Labrum IV, MD, Nashville, TN, and Ian R. Byram, MD, Franklin, TN.)
Radiography is the preferred standard imaging modality for the diagnosis of rotator cuff
calcific tendinopathy.
The acromiohumeral interval should be assessed on AP radiographs.
The acromiohumeral interval normally is 7 to 14 mm (Figure 3).

Figure 3
AP radiograph of a shoulder demonstrates the acromiohumeral interval. Normally, this
interval is 7 to 14 mm. A decreased acromiohumeral interval (6 mm or less) is a radiographic
marker of rotator cuff disease. (Courtesy of Joseph T. Labrum IV, MD, Nashville, TN, and Ian
R. Byram, MD, Franklin, TN.)
An acromiohumeral interval of 6 mm or less is considered pathognomonic for rotator cuff
pathology (Figure 4).
Acetabularization of the acromion, rounding of the greater tuberosity, and femoralization
of the humeral head are signs of rotator cuff arthropathy.
Chronic changes observed on radiographs may obviate the need for MRI to diagnose
rotator cuff dysfunction.

Figure 4
AP radiograph of a right shoulder demonstrates advanced rotator cuff arthropathy, or
degenerative changes secondary to chronic rotator cuff disease. A decreased
acromiohumeral interval, acetabularization of the acromion, a nonconcentric glenohumeral
articulation, and rounding of the greater tuberosity are observed. (Courtesy of Joseph T.
Labrum IV, MD, Nashville, TN, and Ian R. Byram, MD, Franklin, TN.)
Arthritic changes within the glenohumeral joint—joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis,
osteophyte formation, loose bodies, subchondral cysts—can be recognized on radiographs.
Chronic rotator cuff insufficiency may result in anterosuperior escape (migration of the
humeral head through the rotator interval). This results from failure of the subscapularis
and/or supraspinatus (rotator interval lesion).

Radiography
Plain radiographs of the shoulder are the preferred standard imaging modality in the
initial work up of shoulder pathology and should be obtained in all patients undergoing
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Rotator Cuff Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000616
6/19

evaluation for shoulder pain. A standard shoulder series should include orthogonal
views of the shoulder, including a true AP view in the scapular plane, an AP view, an
axillary view, and a scapular-Y view. Although radiographs do not afford direct
visualization of the rotator cuff, several findings are pathognomonic of rotator cuff
disease.
Calcifications noted within the rotator cuff insertional footprint are representative of
rotator cuff calcific tendinopathy. This radiographic finding is caused by deposition of
calcium carbonate apatite within the rotator cuff tendon.
An abnormal acromiohumeral interval, which normally is 7 to 14 mm, indicates superior
migration of the humeral head resulting from rotator cuff disease. Therefore, an
acromiohumeral interval of 6 mm or less is considered pathognomonic for rotator cuff
pathology.
In patients with a decreased acromiohumeral interval, degenerative changes noted
within the glenohumeral joint often represent rotator cuff arthropathy, a term used for
glenohumeral osteoarthritis arising secondary to chronic rotator cuff disease.
Acetabularization of the acromion, rounding of the greater tuberosity, and
femoralization of the humeral head are signs of advanced rotator cuff arthropathy that
can be appreciated on shoulder radiographs.
Chronic changes consistent with rotator cuff arthropathy are apparent on radiographs,
which may obviate the need for MRI in the diagnosis of rotator cuff disease. Chronic
rotator cuff insufficiency may result in anterosuperior escape, a term used to describe
superior migration of the humeral head through the rotator interval. This pathology
often results from failure of the subscapularis and/or supraspinatus, referred to as a
rotator interval lesion.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is an extremely useful imaging modality for evaluation of the rotator cuff

Advantages
Immediate data to the clinician and patient
Cost-effective compared with MRI1 (Resource 2)
Noninvasive imaging modality
Useful in patients with contraindications to or who refuse to undergo other diagnostic
imaging (eg, those with prohibitive implants or pacemakers, claustrophobia, iodinated
contrast allergy)
Accurate for the detection of complete and partial rotator cuff tears (Figure 5)
Figure 5
Coronal ultrasonographic images show an intact (arrow, A) and torn (arrow, B) supraspinatus
tendon. (Reproduced from Schiffern SC, Hamid N: Imaging of the shoulder and elbow, in
Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 742-750.)
Allows for visualization of the rotator cuff in the postoperative setting without substantial
image artifact
Dynamic in nature, allowing for visualization of tendon mobility
Disadvantages
Highly dependent on the technician and equipment factors
Requires movement of the shoulder during examination, which may be difficult in a painful
shoulder
Ultrasonography is not as precise and has limitations compared with MRI

Ultrasonography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Rotator Cuff Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000616
8/19

Ultrasonography is an extremely useful imaging modality for evaluation of rotator cuff
disease. It is highly accurate in detecting full-thickness (92.3% sensitivity and 94.4%
specificity) and partial-thickness (66.7% sensitivity and 93.5% specificity) rotator cuff
tears.1 In addition to being accurate, ultrasonography is a noninvasive, cost-efficient
imaging modality that is well tolerated by patients in the office setting and is associated
with minimal contraindications. Ultrasonography can be used to image the rotator cuff
in patients with metal implants that likely would obscure MRI. Ultrasonography also
allows for a dynamic examination, which may be useful in the setting of revision rotator
cuff repair. Patients undergoing ultrasonographic examination of the shoulder often are
more satisfied than those who undergo MRI.2 The limitations of ultrasonographic
imaging of the shoulder include an inability to visualize intra-articular structures and the
need for shoulder manipulation during examination, which may be poorly tolerated in
some patients with a painful shoulder. In addition, ultrasonography is highly technician
dependent, which may lead to variability in its clinical utility.
Computed Tomography
Has limited utility in visualizing soft-tissue pathology related to rotator cuff disease
Can be used to evaluate the rotator cuff musculature and may demonstrate some degree of
muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (Figure 6)

Figure 6
Sagittal CT scan of a shoulder shows rotator cuff atrophy secondary to rotator cuff disease.
(Courtesy of Joseph T. Labrum IV, MD, Nashville, TN, and Ian R. Byram, MD, Franklin, TN.)
The Goutallier classification of fatty degeneration was originally described using CT scans.
Highly useful for assessing bony anatomy of the shoulder girdle
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction images are the preferred imaging study for
determining version and assessing glenoid bone stock.
In patients with a low likelihood of rotator cuff pathology, CT alone may provide sufficient
information regarding rotator cuff pathology.

Computed Tomography
Evaluation of the rotator cuff and surrounding soft tissue of the shoulder on
nonarthrographic CT scans is relatively limited. CT can be performed to evaluate the
rotator cuff musculature for atrophy or fatty infiltration. In patients with a low likelihood
of rotator cuff pathology, CT alone may provide sufficient information regarding rotator
cuff pathology. CT may be pivotal in assessing glenoid version and glenoid bone stock in
patients with rotator cuff arthropathy secondary to chronic rotator cuff disease. Three-

9/3/26, 4:24 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000616
10/19

dimensional CT reconstruction images of the shoulder girdle allow for clear definition of
the bony anatomy for preoperative planning before shoulder arthroplasty.
CT Arthrography
CT arthrography involves CT performed after injection of iodinated contrast into the
glenohumeral joint.
Arthrography allows for visualization of full-thickness rotator cuff tears that communicate with
the articular surface via the migration of contrast into these pathologic regions (Figure 7).
Figure 7
CT arthrogram of a shoulder shows a rotator cuff tear. (Courtesy of Joseph T. Labrum IV, MD,
Nashville, TN, and Ian R. Byram, MD, Franklin, TN.)
CT arthrography effectively identifies pathology of the intra-articular long head of the biceps
(LHB) and the labrum.
Advantages
Rapid imaging modality
Useful in assessing rotator cuff pathology in the setting of anatomic total shoulder
arthroplasty if concern for rotator cuff failure exists
MRI is limited in the evaluation of rotator cuff failure after total shoulder arthroplasty
secondary to metal artifact limiting the quality of the imaging study.

May be performed in patients in whom MRI is contraindicated (pacemaker, spinal cord
stimulator, bladder stimulator)
Disadvantages
Invasive procedure
Less sensitive visualization of soft tissue surrounding the glenohumeral joint
Ionizing radiation exposure

CT Arthrography
Arthrography involves imaging studies obtained after the injection of iodinated contrast
into the glenohumeral joint. Arthrography is highly effective in aiding evaluation of intra-
articular pathology and rotator cuff tears. CT arthrography allows for visualization of full-
thickness and articular-sided rotator cuff tears via extravasation of iodinated contrast on
imaging studies. CT arthrography requires an invasive procedure and ionizing radiation
exposure. Although CT arthrography is less sensitive in visualizing soft tissue
surrounding the glenohumeral joint, it may be highly useful in patients with
contraindications to MRI or who have possible rotator cuff failure after anatomic total
shoulder arthroplasty because minimal metal artifact obscures image quality.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Indications
Suspected rotator cuff or soft-tissue pathology
Inadequate visualization with other imaging modalities
Diagnostic accuracy
Full-thickness rotator cuff tear: 92.1% sensitivity and 92.9% specificity; partial-thickness
rotator cuff tear: 63.6% sensitivity and 91.7% specificity.3
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating rotator cuff tears and postoperative
healing.1
Rotator cuff pathology—A wide spectrum of rotator cuff disease can be visualized on MRIs
(Figure 8).
Rotator cuff tears are best visualized on T2-weighted MRIs.
Rotator cuff tear retraction is best appreciated on coronal plane reconstructions.

The width of the tear and the degree of muscle belly atrophy is best visualized on sagittal
reconstructions.
Rotator cuff muscle atrophy and fatty degeneration are best assessed on T1-weighted
sagittal MRIs at the level of the base of the coracoid process (Figure 9).

thickness rotator cuff tear (arrow). C, Full- thickness, nonretracted rotator cuff tear (arrow).
D, Massive, retracted rotator cuff tear (arrow). (Reproduced from Schiffern SC, Hamid N:

LHB pathology
The LHB tendon is best visualized on axial MRIs.
Medial dislocation of the LHB out of the bicipital groove may indicate a subscapularis tear
(Figure 10).

Humeral avulsion of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (HAGL)
Best visualized on coronal oblique T2-weighted, fat-suppressed MRIs acutely postinjury
Consider magnetic resonance arthrography in patients with a delayed presentation
J-sign on MRI is considered pathognomonic for HAGL
Advantages
Global assessment of all shoulder structures, including cartilage and bone marrow
Ideal visualization of soft tissues

Disadvantages
Cost (often requires insurance preapproval)
Claustrophobia
Contraindication secondary to pacemaker or other implantable devices or metallic implants

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for rotator cuff disease in the
native shoulder. MRI evaluation is associated with a 92.1% sensitivity and a 92.9%
specificity for full-thickness rotator cuff tears and a 63.6% sensitivity and 91.7%
specificity for partial-thickness rotator cuff tears.1 Indications for MRI of the shoulder
include suspected rotator cuff disease or other soft-tissue pathology of the shoulder
girdle. Rotator cuff tears are best visualized on T2-weighted MRIs. Tear retraction
typically is best visualized on the coronal MRIs. Rotator cuff muscle belly atrophy typically
is best visualized on T1-weighted sagittal reconstructions at the level of the coracoid
base. In addition to ideal visualization of the rotator cuff, MRI also provides detail of the
other soft-tissue structures surrounding the glenohumeral joint, including the glenoid
labrum, the LHB tendon, cartilage, and bone marrow. The LHB tendon is best visualized
on axial MRIs, with edema or an intra-substance signal indicating pathology. Medial
dislocation of the LHB out of the bicipital groove may indicate a subscapularis tear.
HAGL also may be detected on MRI. These injuries commonly arise in patients with other
shoulder pathology (rotator cuff tear, glenoid labral pathology, shoulder instability) and
may be a cause of recurrent glenohumeral instability. The inferior glenohumeral
ligament can be avulsed from the anterior (most common) or posterior aspect of the
humerus and can be appreciated on MRI/magnetic resonance arthrography as an
elongation and more gradual curvature of the capsule at the inferomedial aspect of the
humeral neck. This often is described as the J-sign and is considered pathognomic for a
HAGL lesion. Disadvantages of MRI include high cost, which often requires insurance
preapproval; patient discomfort (claustrophobia); and numerous contraindications
secondary to implanted devices.

9/3/26, 4:24 PM

Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
Magnetic resonance arthrography involves MRI performed after the injection of iodinated
contrast into the glenohumeral joint.
Magnetic resonance arthrography is ideal for detailed evaluation of intra-articular
glenohumeral pathology (partial-thickness rotator cuff tears, glenoid labrum pathology,
delayed presentation of HAGL, and biceps abnormalities).
Magnetic resonance arthrography is more accurate than conventional MRI in assessment of
postoperative shoulder pathology.
Diagnostic accuracy3
Full-thickness rotator cuff tear: 95.4% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity
Partial-thickness rotator cuff tear: 85.9% sensitivity and 96% specificity
Mark as Complete
